newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin tells politicians to stop squabbling.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin tells politicians to stop squabbling.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, sounding confident ahead of next month's planned heart surgery, on Friday ordered state officials to stop squabbling and start working to regain the trust of ordinary Russians.

But in a sign of the daunting problems awaiting the elite, Defence Minister Igor Rodionov -- under mounting pressure from his subordinates -- said Russia's cash-strapped armed forces were on the brink of "uncontrollable developments".

Policy makers also received a stinging rebuke from the International Monetary Fund, whose mission, worried about low tax collection, has left Moscow without agreeing to cough up more cash for Russia's market reforms.

"I want to remind the politicians Russia has made its choice for the next four years," Yeltsin said in a five-minute radio address apparently recorded in the Barvikha sanitorium where he is preparing for his bypass operation.
"There have been enough struggles for influence, fights for jobs, criticism and electioneering. It is time to work...
"While each player only plays his own pipe we will only be marking time and will lose the people's trust," Yeltsin said in a clear, confident voice.
A date for the operation has not been fixed but doctors, apparently satisfied with the president's overall condition, say it will probably take place in the latter half of November.
A senior Yeltsin adviser said the president's aides were restricting their own contact with the Russian leader to try to help him prepare for the surgery.
Rodionov's comments pinpointed the plight of the once powerful armed forces after years of underfunding which have driven many soldiers to beg on the streets and forced officers to take other jobs.
In a speech to army veterans, Rodionov said a shortage of funds, appalling social conditions and poor maintenance were leading to a "severe crisis".

"Russia's leadership and society should know that the chronic lack of funds is taking the armed forces to the brink of undesirable, and even uncontrollable, developments," Interfax news agency quoted Rodionov as saying.
"If the 1997 defence budget is not changed, Russia may lose the armed forces as an integral and active state structure, with all the consequences which would follow that," he said.
Rodionov's speech coincided with a deadline set by a group of general staff officers, who threatened to use force if overdue wages were not paid.

The ultimatum, laid down in an open letter by the unnamed officers published last week, urged Rodionov to tackle those in the government it said were set on ruining Russia and surrendering it to the West.
"We have enough force to make these gentlemen abandon their plans," said the letter in the Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily.
There was no further word from the officers on Friday, but Rodionov's speech clearly reflected their concerns.

The State Duma lower house of parliament has rejected the budget and ministers say a new draft being discussed will give the military more money. But the budget deficit will stay the same and it is not clear where the money will come from.
Russia's former national security supremo, Alexander Lebed, sacked by President Boris Yeltsin last week, has warned that the armed forces were on the brink of rebellion.
Lebed's warning, dismissed by Rodionov at the time, gave a dramatic twist to a fierce battle for influence that has accompanied Yeltsin's prolonged absence from the Kremlin.
